sn51.1:1.1: _Iddhi_ (Sanskrit _ṛddhi_ or _siddhi_) conveys the root sense “thriving, increase, success”. In the Atharva Veda we find _samṛddhi_ and _vyṛddhi_  in the sense “prosperity” and “misfortune” (eg. 10.2.10). As “success, completion” (of the sacrifice) we find _ṛddhi_ at Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.6.9.11. As far as I know, the Buddhist texts are where we first find _iddhi_ in the sense of “psychic power” (or “spiritual magnification”, “heightened potency”; [sn51.10:3.2](), [sn51.11:5.1]()). This sense is not attested in Sanskrit texts until later, where we find eight such powers mentioned (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.20.53, 9.21.12). The Yogasūtra elaborates many such powers and the methods of achieving them (3.17–3.37), but immediately warns that they are obstacles to _samādhi_ (3.38). They are sometimes also numbered eight in Jain texts, which list various kinds of _ṛddhi_ (or _labdhi_; eg. Ṭhāṇaṅga 5.168, Bhagavatisūtra 8.139). Perhaps this idea was first popularized among the _śramaṇa_ schools such as Buddhism and Jainism. All these religions, however, aim at liberation from suffering, and do not regard the attainment of psychic powers as an end in itself. Probably the interest in such abilities was drawn from the broader ascetic culture, where to this day we find a fascination with such powers. In the Indian context, it is important to avoid such terms as “supernatural”, as such phenomena, though extraordinary, are well within the realm of the natural. They do not arise from the intervention of God or any other metaphysical means, but rather from the development and amplification of abilities latent in all beings. This teaching framework, accordingly, focuses on those things that form the *bases* (_pāda_) of psychic power. The powers themselves are mere adornments to the path, whose true purpose is to lead “from the near shore to the far shore”.
sn51.1:1.3: “Enthusiasm” (_chanda_) is skillful desire to accomplish the path. The word _chanda_ itself is neutral, and sometimes means “sensual desire” (_kāmacchanda_) or “consent” ([pli-tv-kd2:23.1.5](), [pli-tv-bi-pm:9.1]()).
sn51.1:1.4: The four factors map straightforwardly onto the final three factors of the noble eightfold path. “Enthusiasm” and “energy” both fall under “right effort”, while _citta_ is “right immersion”, and _vīmaṁsā_ is “right wisdom”.
sn51.1:1.5: Here, _citta_ (“mental development”) means the development of the mind in immersion. This sense is common for _citta_ in the context of the path, for example _cittasampadā_ = _samādhisampadā_ ([dn8:15.2]()); _cittabhāvanā_ = _samādhibhāvanā_ ([sn1.23:2.2]()). The same sense is apparent in _cittānupassanā_ (“observation of the mind”) in _satipaṭṭhāna_, although there we see that the sense is somewhat broader, encompassing the mind as it goes through the process of development leading to immersion.
